response.passage: Rohan is helping his father design a triangular flower bed for their new shop entrance. The sides of the triangular plot measure 13 meters, 14 meters, and 15 meters. To calculate the area, Rohan first finds the semi-perimeter by adding the three sides and dividing the total by two, which gives him 21 meters. He then uses Heron's formula, calculating the square root of the product of the semi-perimeter and the differences between the semi-perimeter and each side. He carefully subtracts each side length from 21 individually before multiplying. Meanwhile, his neighbor is building a decorative rhombus-shaped sign for the shop. The neighbor mistakenly thinks the area is simply the product of the diagonals, but Rohan explains that the area is actually half the product of the diagonals. Rohan also reminds him that for any triangle, the height is not necessarily one of the sides, so one must use the perpendicular distance from the vertex to the opposite base. Finally, Rohan notes that all measurements must be converted to the same unit, such as meters, before performing any calculations to ensure the area is accurate.
response.summary: Rohan calculates the area of a triangular flower bed using Heron's formula by first finding the semi-perimeter. He also clarifies common geometric misconceptions regarding rhombus areas, triangle heights, and unit consistency.
